response_text: PendSV is set to the lowest interrupt priority, and it is pended by SVC (via yield) only after SVC completes, so the context switch occurs in a clean, tail end interrupt with no higher-priority ISR preemption of the switch itself. On entry to PendSV, the Cortex-M hardware has already auto-stacked {r0–r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR} to the current thread’s PSP. The assembly stub then saves the remaining callee-saved registers r4–r11 to that same PSP stack frame and calls the C scheduler: Save current thread: osSched() stores the current thread’s PSP into its TCB. Pick next thread: osSched() selects the next READY TCB (front of the ready queue) and loads its saved PSP into a CPU register for restore. Restore next thread: Back in PendSV, the stub sets LR to an EXC_RETURN value that returns to Thread mode using PSP (0xFFFFFFFD), pops r4–r11 from the next thread’s stack, writes PSP, and BX LR. The exception return causes hardware to unstack {r0–r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR} from that same PSP, resuming the chosen thread exactly where it left off. This split—tiny, deterministic assembly for save/restore plus C for policy in osSched, keeps the CPU-specific pieces minimal while letting you express scheduling logic clearly.\n
